notes.h: Base level and the graded river
notes.b: A river can erode no lower than its base level, the lowest point it can cut down to. Sea level is the ultimate base level, and a river that has settled into balance with its base level has a smooth, predictable shape.
points: A lake, a band of resistant rock or a main river (for its tributary, the smaller stream that joins it) acts as a temporary, local base level, because the river cannot cut below that point until it is removed.

A graded (equilibrium) profile is a smooth, concave long profile (the river's slope from source to mouth, steep at the top and flattening downstream) where the river's energy is just enough to carry its load (the material it transports), so erosion and deposition (dropping of load) are balanced.
A change in base level upsets this balance, so the river adjusts its profile to the new level.
notes.tip: Define a graded profile as one where erosion and deposition are balanced, and say that a change in base level upsets this balance.

notes.b: Rejuvenation is renewed vertical erosion (cutting downwards) caused by a fall in base level relative to the land. It gives the river renewed energy and interrupts a cycle of erosion.
points: Cause 1, a eustatic fall in sea level (the sea itself moves): during a glacial period, water is locked up in ice sheets, so sea level falls worldwide and the river has further to fall to reach the sea.

Cause 2, isostatic uplift (the land itself moves): land depressed under the weight of an ice sheet rises, or rebounds, when the ice melts, raising it relative to sea level. There is more on this in Glaciation.
Cause 3, tectonic uplift of the land by earth movements, which raises the land above its old base level so the river cuts down again.

Cause 4, an increase in discharge (the volume of water flowing in the river), e.g. from a wetter climate or by river capture (one river taking over the water of another), gives the river more energy; this is a less common cause.
notes.tip: If asked for the name of the process by which a river in its lower course begins to erode again after a change in base level, answer rejuvenation. It follows a fall in base level relative to the land; a rise causes drowning and deposition instead. Do not swap eustatic (the sea moves) and isostatic (the land moves).

notes.b: A fall in base level is felt first at the river's mouth (where it meets the sea), and the effect then travels up the valley. This leaves a river made of two parts.
points: Rejuvenation begins at the mouth and works upstream by headward erosion (erosion that cuts back towards the source), because the extra energy is first available at the lowest point.
For a long time the river has two graded sections: a new, steeper lower section and the old, gentler upper section.
This is the landscape that is temporarily out of balance, because the two sections reflect two different base levels.

notes.b: A knickpoint is where the new, rejuvenated river meets the old one. It is the key feature of a rejuvenated long profile (the river's slope from source to mouth).
points: 1. Rejuvenation cuts down at the mouth, creating a new graded section below the old one.
2. Where the new and old graded profiles meet, the long profile has a break of slope: this is the knickpoint.
3. A waterfall or rapids is often found at the knickpoint, because the river drops steeply there. The knickpoint is the break of slope itself, not the waterfall.
4. The knickpoint retreats upstream over time, and the new profile extends behind it.
5. Once the whole river has graded to the new base level, the knickpoint disappears.
Diagram: long profile showing the old and new graded sections and the knickpoint at their junction.
notes.tip: If asked what a knickpoint is, say it is a break of slope on the long profile where the new and old graded profiles meet. Do not define it as a waterfall; a waterfall or rapids is what is found at it. Here the waterfall is caused by the change in base level, whatever the rock.

notes.b: Renewed vertical erosion cuts existing meanders (bends in the river) down into the land, rather than forming them on a floodplain (the flat land beside a river). This leaves meanders set deep in a valley with steep sides.
points: Ingrown meanders have an asymmetrical cross-section (a slice across the valley), with one gentle and one steep side, because downcutting is slower and there is some lateral (sideways) erosion.
Entrenched meanders have a symmetrical cross-section with steep sides, forming a gorge (a deep, narrow, steep-sided valley), because downcutting is rapid.
Example of entrenched meanders: the Goosenecks of the San Juan River, Utah, USA.
Example of incised meanders: the River Wye, Wales-England border.
Diagram: cross-section showing a meander cut down into the land, with steep sides and no floodplain.
notes.tip: Incised meanders are not ordinary meanders: they are cut down into solid rock with steep valley sides, not formed on a floodplain. In a labelled diagram, include an incised meander.

notes.b: When a river cuts down into its old floodplain, the old floodplain is left stranded above the river. River terraces are remnants of an old floodplain, left as flat steps above the new floodplain after the river has cut down.
points: Paired terraces are at the same height on both sides of the valley; they form where the river downcuts rapidly, so it has little time to move sideways.
Unpaired terraces are at different heights on each side; they form while the river downcuts and migrates (moves) sideways.
Example: the river terraces of the River Thames in and around London, England.
Diagram: cross-section of a valley showing paired terraces above the present floodplain.
notes.tip: Paired terraces is a label exams use on a rejuvenation diagram. River terraces are not terracettes (small steps made by soil creep) and not kame terraces (made by meltwater from glaciers).

notes.b: Uplift of the land gives a river renewed cutting power, and deep incision (cutting down) can produce a gorge, a deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
points: A gorge can be cut by deep incision of a river into an uplifted landscape.
Example: the Grand Canyon, cut by the Colorado River in Arizona, USA, as the Colorado Plateau was uplifted.

notes.h: Reading rejuvenation features on a diagram
notes.b: Each episode of rejuvenation leaves a mark, so a diagram can be read like a record. Counting the marks tells you how many times the river has been rejuvenated.
points: The number of rejuvenations equals the number of knickpoints on a long profile, because each fall in base level creates one.
On a cross-section, the number of rejuvenations equals the number of terrace levels above the present floodplain, because each rejuvenation leaves a terrace behind.
Rejuvenation features not shown in a diagram are knickpoints, waterfalls or rapids at knickpoints, incised meanders, river terraces and gorges.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to count the number of rejuvenations shown in a diagram, and to name two rejuvenation features not shown. Pick two from the list that are missing from the diagram.

notes.h: Rise in base level and the coast
notes.b: A rise in base level, from sea level rising or land sinking, reduces the river's energy. This is the opposite of rejuvenation, so it drowns rather than cuts.
points: The lower course is drowned and deposition (dropping of load) increases because the river has less energy; the mouth becomes a ria (a drowned river valley) or an estuary (the wide tidal mouth of a river). There is more on rias in Glaciation.
Coastal landforms caused by a change in base level are raised beaches (from a fall in base level) and rias (from a rise).

Setting: rivers of north-west Ireland were rejuvenated as the land rose isostatically after the Midlandian ice melted about 10,000 years ago; the north, under thicker ice, rose more, with raised beaches at Malin Head, Co. Donegal.
notes.tip: A rise in base level causes drowning and deposition, not rejuvenation. If asked to name two coastal landforms formed by an adjustment to base level, give raised beaches and rias.

keyTerms.definition: The lowest level to which a river can erode; sea level is the ultimate base level.
A smooth, concave long profile on which the river's energy is just enough to carry its load, balancing erosion and deposition.
Renewed vertical erosion by a river in its lower course, caused by a fall in base level relative to the land.
A worldwide change in sea level, such as the fall caused by water locked up in ice sheets.
The break of slope on a long profile where the new and old graded profiles meet, which retreats upstream over time.
An incised meander with an asymmetrical cross-section, cut down slowly with some lateral erosion.
An incised meander with a symmetrical, steep-sided gorge cross-section, cut down rapidly.
A meander cut down vertically into the land by renewed erosion after rejuvenation.
A flat step left above the present floodplain, the remnant of an older floodplain.
River terraces at the same height on both sides of a valley, formed by rapid downcutting.
River terraces at different heights on each side of a valley, formed while the river downcuts and migrates sideways.
A deep, steep-sided valley cut by a river, in rejuvenation, into uplifted land.
A beach left above present sea level by a fall in base level, such as isostatic uplift.
A drowned river valley formed by a rise in base level, with the lower course flooded by the sea.

factCards.term: Base level: ultimate vs temporary, with three temporary examples
factCards.definition: Sea level is the ultimate base level. A lake, a band of resistant rock, or the main river (for its tributary) acts as a temporary, local base level.

A eustatic fall in sea level, as water is locked in ice sheets in a glacial period; isostatic uplift, as land pressed down by ice rises after it melts; tectonic uplift by earth movements; less commonly, more discharge from a wetter climate or river capture.

factCards.term: Rejuvenation: how it spreads along a river
factCards.definition: It begins at the mouth and works upstream by headward erosion. For a long time the river has two graded sections, a new, steeper lower one and the old, gentler upper one, reflecting two base levels: a landscape temporarily out of balance.

factCards.term: Knickpoint: how it forms and changes over time
factCards.definition: Rejuvenation cuts down from the mouth, making a new graded section below the old one; where they meet, a break of slope forms, often with a waterfall or rapids; it retreats upstream over time and disappears once the whole river grades to the new base level.

factCards.term: Incised meanders: how they form, with two examples
factCards.definition: Renewed vertical erosion after base level falls cuts existing meanders down into the land, leaving them in steep-sided valleys with no floodplain. Examples: the River Wye, Wales–England border; the Goosenecks of the San Juan River, Utah, USA (entrenched).

factCards.term: River terraces: how they form, with an example
factCards.definition: First, base level falls and the river cuts down into its own floodplain; then it forms a new floodplain at the lower level; remnants of the old floodplain are left as flat steps above it. Example: the River Thames in and around London, England.

factCards.term: Gorge from uplift: name an example and how it formed
factCards.definition: The Grand Canyon, Arizona, USA, cut by deep incision of the Colorado River as the Colorado Plateau was uplifted.

factCards.term: Rejuvenation diagram: how to count the number of rejuvenations
factCards.definition: On a long profile, count the knickpoints: one per rejuvenation. On a valley cross-section, count the terrace levels above the present floodplain: one per rejuvenation.

factCards.term: Name five rejuvenation features to give when asked for features not shown
factCards.definition: Knickpoint; a waterfall or rapids at the knickpoint; incised meanders; river terraces (e.g. paired terraces); gorge.

factCards.term: Rise in base level: effects on a river and its mouth
factCards.definition: Sea level rising, or land sinking, reduces the river's energy; the lower course is drowned, deposition increases and the mouth becomes a ria or an estuary. Coastal landforms from changes in base level: raised beaches (a fall) and rias (a rise).

factCards.term: Rivers of north-west Ireland: why they were rejuvenated
factCards.definition: The land rose isostatically after the Midlandian ice melted about 10,000 years ago. The north, under thicker ice, rose more, as shown by raised beaches at Malin Head, Co. Donegal.

questions.prompt: Examine how a fall in base level can affect a river and its landforms.
questions.model: Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode, and sea level is the ultimate base level. A fall in base level relative to the land gives the river renewed energy, so it erodes vertically again; this is rejuvenation. Causes include a eustatic fall in sea level, when water is locked up in ice sheets during a glacial period, and isostatic uplift, when land depressed under ice rises after the ice melts. Tectonic uplift and an increase in discharge are further causes. Rejuvenation begins at the mouth and works upstream by headward erosion, so the river has a new, steeper lower section and an old upper section. Where the two graded profiles meet there is a knickpoint, a break of slope often marked by a waterfall or rapids. The knickpoint retreats upstream as the river downcuts, and the river's landforms adjust as it does so. Incised meanders form when renewed vertical erosion cuts existing meanders down into the land. Ingrown meanders have an asymmetrical cross-section and downcut slowly with some lateral erosion. Entrenched meanders have a symmetrical, steep-sided gorge cross-section and downcut rapidly, as at the Goosenecks of the San Juan River, Utah, USA. River terraces are flat steps left above the new floodplain when the river cuts down. Paired terraces at the same height on both sides form where downcutting is rapid. Unpaired terraces at different heights form while the river migrates sideways as it downcuts. The number of terrace levels above the present floodplain shows how many rejuvenations have occurred. A labelled diagram should show the old and new graded sections, the knickpoint, an incised meander and paired terraces.

questions.prompt: Explain what a knickpoint is and describe how it changes over time.
questions.model: A knickpoint is the break of slope on a long profile where the new, steeper graded profile below meets the old graded profile above. A waterfall or rapids is often found at the knickpoint. As the river downcuts to the new base level, the knickpoint retreats upstream by headward erosion, so the new graded section extends behind it. Eventually the knickpoint reaches the head of the river and disappears once the whole river has graded to the new base level.

questions.prompt: Name two causes of river rejuvenation.
questions.model: A eustatic fall in sea level, caused by water being locked up in ice sheets, and isostatic uplift of the land after the ice melts. Tectonic uplift is also accepted.
